papers.title: Why do continual physical learners need sleep?
papers.abstract: Sleep is widespread across the animal kingdom, including in organisms without a centralized nervous system. Does learning create a need for sleep, even without biology? To explore this question, we study a disordered spring network trained to perform a sequence of mechanical allosteric tasks through local changes in bond stiffness. We find that continual learning progressively reduces the network's ability to acquire new tasks as individual bonds become increasingly specialized. We identify an exact algebraic relationship between the polarization of bond dominance and the network's remaining learning capacity, providing a quantitative measure of this loss of adaptability. We then demonstrate that random internal perturbations allow individual bonds to estimate their mechanical dominance and locally adjust their stiffnesses to restore learning capacity. However, the forces associated with active learning bias these local measurements and interfere with restoration. Separating learning and repair into wake-like and sleep-like phases removes this interference and improves continual-learning performance. Our results suggest that the need for offline restorative phases can emerge from the mechanics of physical learning, even in systems without biological components.

papers.title: Spontaneous axis formation through defect fusion in active nematics
papers.abstract: Initially spherical embryos break symmetry to establish a body axis. Topological defects in tissue nematic order have been implicated in axis formation, but the physical mechanisms underlying defect organization in active materials remain unclear. We study an active nematic fluid on a sphere using a fully covariant hydrodynamic theory that ensures thermodynamic consistency in the passive limit. We find that, in compressible systems, active nematic traction drives a spontaneous transition from the equilibrium configuration of four separated +1/2 defects to two antipodal +1 defects through pairwise fusion. The resulting state defines an axis, with aster or vortex textures at the poles depending on the flow-nematic coupling. These results identify a physical mechanism by which active forces reorganize topological defects to establish an axis on a spherical surface.

papers.title: A Butterfly-Inspired Agent Learns to Climb with Self-Generated Wingbeats
papers.abstract: Butterfly free climbing involves dynamic coupling between wing motion and unsteady aerodynamic forces that drive the animal's ascent. Four-wing coordination determines how these forces combine to support weight and direct propulsion. How aerodynamic feedback shapes such coordination remains difficult to establish when wing kinematics are prescribed in experiments and simulations. Here, we construct a virtual flight environment with rapid aerodynamic feedback and train a butterfly-inspired agent using the soft actor-critic algorithm. Without a wingbeat generator, the agent spontaneously develops non-sinusoidal wingbeats and achieves reward-directed climbing. The climbing angle varies primarily with wingbeat frequency and mean angle of attack, and force-balance analysis links these adaptations to gravity projections along and normal to the flight direction. The aerodynamic forces are faithfully recovered only when the agent-generated wing motions are reconstructed with higher-order harmonics, rather than the commonly used first harmonic. Independent and combined modulation of frequency and mean angle of attack further reveals their nonlinear coupling in regulating climbing direction. These findings reveal how coordinated propulsion strategies emerge under physical constraints and provide a theoretical framework for studying strategy formation through interactions between organisms and their fluid environment.

papers.title: Stability of Homochiral Peptides in Capillary Environments: Implications for the Origin of Biological Homochirality
papers.abstract: The homochiral proteins in living organisms are rather stable, but they tend to lose their secondary conformations and homochiral order over time. This instability is found in all living organisms, from bacteria to humans. The aging of living organisms, with the destruction of their vital homochiral order, raises the questions about the emergence of homochirality and how the homochiral order in the building molecules was ensured in prebiotic times before life evolved. Based on thermodynamic arguments, we propose that the homochiral order was achieved by a ``Frank-synthesis'' of homochiral peptides from racemic amino acids and in a capillary environment in the vents in the Earth's crust, perhaps at crystalline chiral surfaces, and that the peptides are stable over long times in such an environment. The $hypothesis$ can be confirmed by experimental analysis of the stability of the secondary structures in proteins as a function of water activity and in a capillary environment.

papers.title: Nonreciprocal Hopfield nets for angiogenesis
papers.abstract: During sprouting angiogenesis, endothelial cells dynamically reorganize among three relevant phenotypes (glycolytic, stalk and tip) to form new blood vessels, with cells transitioning from one phenotype to another. These cell-state transitions may involve intrinsic nonequilibrium dynamics that go beyond relaxation of the conventional Waddington landscape. We investigate this possibility using a nonreciprocal Hopfield network inferred from single-cell RNA sequencing and RNA velocity data for 1896 endothelial cells on a panel of 1873 genes. We encode the three experimentally identified phenotypes as correlated memory patterns and introduce an asymmetric mixing matrix describing their effective interactions. A dynamical mean- field reduction yields a three-dimensional system for the overlaps with these phenotypic memories, whose parameters are fitted to RNA-velocity-derived trajectories. The nonreciprocal model outperforms its reciprocal counterpart on held-out testing data. Remarkably, its long-time dynamics exhibit either stationary attractors or sustained cycles connecting phenotypic states, depending on the inference timescale. These results suggest that angiogenic cell fate decisions may involve directed, non-relaxational dynamics that cannot be captured by a conventional energy landscape. This approach may also provide a useful framework for investigating how perturbations constrain cellular differentiation.

papers.title: A free-energy approach for stochastic reaction-drift-diffusion lattice simulations of crowded biological systems
papers.abstract: Molecular size alters spatial distributions, reaction equilibria, and transport in crowded mixtures, but resolving individual particle encounters can make large stochastic simulations computationally costly. We developed a lattice-based framework for simulating reaction-drift-diffusion systems with volume exclusion captured as a free energy functional in each voxel. Changes in this free energy, together with external one-body potentials, modify diffusion and reaction propensities. Our framework accommodates mixtures of particle sizes without resolving each particle's position within a voxel. We implemented our framework in an operator splitting scheme and compared our predictions with off-lattice interacting-particle simulations. Inclusion of the local free energy functional improved spatial occupancies and shifts in reaction equilibria relative to point-particle simulations. With separate approximations for larger spheres and polymers, we simulated crowding-induced slowing and spatial segregation. We then modeled motor proteins' traffic jams on a structured track representing a microtubule. Our results demonstrate how local composition can inform stochastic reaction and transport rates without resolving individual encounters.

papers.title: Molecular energies from sparse quantum prolate diagonalization on a trapped-ion quantum processor
papers.abstract: We introduce sparse quantum prolate diagonalization (sparse QPD), which combines the original formulation of QPD [Phys. Rev. Res., 8(3), 033177, (2026)] with compressed sensing to exploit Hamiltonian spectrum sparsity for molecular systems. We show that sparse sampling reduces the sample complexity of QPD from $\mathcal{O}(N_s)$ to $\mathcal{O}(\log N_s)$, where $N_s$ is the number of sampled points of the autocorrelation function (i.e.\ distinct circuits), without increasing circuit depth at chemical accuracy. With a two-orbital active-space-embedded Hamiltonian for an interacting arginine--tryptophan residue pair in water as an example, we show that on the Quantinuum Helios trapped-ion quantum computer, sparse QPD resolves the Hamiltonian energies to chemical accuracy with circuits of up to 448 two-qubit gates. For a suitably large quantum processor, we demonstrate numerically in the weakly correlated regime that the method extends to larger systems.

papers.title: QuantumXCT: Learning Interaction-Induced State Transformation in Cell-Cell Communication via Quantum Entanglement and Generative Modeling
papers.abstract: Inferring cell-cell communication (CCC) from single-cell transcriptomic data remains challenging. Most existing methods retrieve curated ligand-receptor pairs, score their coordinated average expression and apply statistical testing, a static and indirect strategy that tends to overlook intracellular signaling consequences, context dependence and higher-order interactions. Here, we introduce QuantumXCT, a hybrid quantum-classical framework that defines CCC as learnable transformations between cellular state distributions induced by cell-cell interaction. By encoding transcriptomic profiles into a high-dimensional Hilbert space, QuantumXCT trains parameterized quantum circuits to learn a unitary transformation mapping a baseline non-interacting cellular state to an interacting state, and infers CCC under explicitly stated modeling assumptions. Unlike methods restricted to curated ligand-receptor pairs, QuantumXCT can evaluate any cross-cell gene pair. On synthetic data with known ground-truth interactions, QuantumXCT ranked the programmed intercellular interactions above non-interacting gene pairs (ROC-AUC 0.93). On an ovarian cancer-fibroblast mono- and co-culture model, it identified a PDGFB-PDGFRB-STAT3 axis reproducible across bootstrap resamples, amplitude encodings and search algorithms, and consistent with published perturbation experiments. The learned circuit is interpretable: its entangling topology translates into interaction networks, and post hoc contribution analysis quantifies the influence of individual interactions on the observed state transitions. QuantumXCT provides an interpretable, hypothesis-generating framework for de novo discovery of communication programs, and delineates both the potential and the current limits of quantum machine learning in single-cell biology.
